 The Kabul Tribune (KT)— Suspected dengue fever cases in 
Afghanistan increased more than fourfold in October compared with the previous 
month, while reported cases of other major diseases declined, the World Health 
Organization said in its latest epidemiological report. 
 The WHO said 1,675 suspected dengue cases and one associated 
death were reported between Oct. 4 and 31, compared with 364 suspected cases 
and no deaths in September. The increase of 360.2% was consistent with the 
usual seasonal trend, the report said. 
 The death was the first dengue-related fatality recorded in 
Afghanistan since January 2026, according to the WHO. 
 Despite the rise in dengue cases, reported infections of 
other diseases declined. Suspected Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever cases fell 
44.1%, confirmed COVID-19 cases dropped 67.7%, acute watery diarrhea cases 
decreased 34.7%, suspected measles cases declined 22.6% and acute respiratory 
infection pneumonia cases fell 3.8%. 
 The WHO cautioned that the monthly comparisons should be 
interpreted carefully because October covered four epidemiological weeks, 
compared with five in September. 
 The report recorded 11,798 cases of acute watery diarrhea 
with dehydration and six associated deaths in October, compared with 18,054 
cases and seven deaths in September. 
 There were also 94,104 cases of acute respiratory infection 
pneumonia and 149 associated deaths, down from 97,848 cases and 191 deaths in 
the previous month. 
 Suspected measles cases totaled 1,152, with five associated 
deaths, compared with 1,489 cases and 13 deaths in September. Confirmed 
COVID-19 cases fell to 42 from 130. No COVID-19-related deaths have been 
reported since January 2026, the WHO said. 
 The report also recorded 123 suspected Crimean-Congo 
hemorrhagic fever cases and three associated deaths, down from 220 cases and 
five deaths in September. 
 Health Services and Disease Surveillance 
 WHO-supported health care facilities provided 117,607 
outpatient consultations and distributed 131 medical kits, reaching more than 
1.9 million beneficiaries, the report said. A total of 498 health workers also 
received training in specialized medical fields. 
 The organization said 16,884 travelers were screened during 
the reporting period to strengthen early disease detection and cross-border 
surveillance. 
 WHO supports a network of 65 primary health care centers 
across 18 provinces, alongside six national specialized infectious disease 
hospitals, a trauma and emergency center, a national mental health hospital and 
five inpatient mental health wards across eight provinces. 
 Its support also includes 11 drug treatment centers and four 
opioid agonist maintenance treatment centers in 13 provinces. 
 Training for health workers covered emergency care, surgical 
site infection prevention, treatment of severe acute malnutrition, mass 
casualty management, laboratory diagnosis of diseases, measles and other 
vaccine-preventable diseases, respiratory infection management, mental 
health-related services, safe blood transfusion and treatment of 
noncommunicable diseases.
